page_title: Understanding UUIDs, ULIDs and String Representations

sources.entry: Understanding UUIDs, ULIDs and String Representations

summary.title: Understanding UUIDs, ULIDs and String Representations
summary.one_liner: Learn why sequential numeric IDs have limits, how random UUIDs fix distribution but lose locality, how ULIDs add a timestamp prefix, and how to encode 128-bit IDs as shorter strings such as Base32 or Base62.
takeaways: Numeric sequence IDs are simple but can overflow (32-bit), are coupled to their table, bottleneck on one generator, and complicate sharding.
Random 128-bit UUIDs allow distributed generation without coordination, with a tiny collision risk, but have no locality, which wastes B-tree index ordering.
ULIDs put a 48-bit millisecond Unix timestamp in the first bits and 80 random bits after, giving time-ordered, collision-resistant IDs.
A 128-bit ID is just a big number, so it can be written as hex UUID, Crockford Base32 (26 chars for ULID), or Base62, which sorts correctly when zero-padded.
summary.summary: The article explains why auto-incrementing numeric IDs (SERIAL/BIGSERIAL) run into size, coupling, scalability and sharding problems. It then covers random UUIDs, their distributed-generation benefits, and their collision and index-locality drawbacks. It proposes ULIDs, which use a 48-bit timestamp plus 80 random bits, and walks through converting a ULID's bits into bytes, hex UUID form, Crockford Base32, and Base62 with worked examples. The author also links Go and Ruby libraries for converting between formats.
